query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In multi-principal element alloys with carefully balanced Al and Cr levels, synergy between these elements drives the formation of stable, continuous Al2O3- and Cr2O3-rich oxide scales, which significantly inhibit oxygen diffusion and cation outflow during high-temperature exposure, thereby providing enhanced oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy (HEA) with minimal precipitates, used as the baseline material (label: HEA_Std).
generation.intervention: Systematically increase Al and Cr in the baseline alloy to create a suite of compositions with controlled Al/Cr ratios.
generation.conditions: Conduct isothermal oxidation tests at 1000 °C in air for 100 h, with periodic weight measurements and subsequent microstructural analysis by SEM/EDS and XRD.
generation.structural_mediator: Simultaneous co-oxidation of Al and Cr forms continuous, slow-growing oxide scales (Al2O3 and Cr2O3) that mitigate further oxygen penetration and metal ion diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, Al and Cr preferentially oxidize at the alloy surface, forming dense oxide layers that block further reaction by minimizing oxygen ingress and metal outward diffusion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to an alloy with low Al/Cr content, the optimized Al-Cr compositions will exhibit markedly lower mass gain over repeated oxidation cycles and more uniform, intact, protective oxides.
generation.baseline: The same multi-principal element alloy without elevated Al and Cr contents, anticipated to form non-protective or discontinuous oxide scales with faster oxidation kinetics.
generation.boundary: For exposures well above 1000 °C or far beyond 100 h, other phase transformations, spallation phenomena, or detrimental oxide volatilities may dominate, reducing the efficacy of the Al/Cr synergy.
generation.uncertainty: Minor reactive elements (e.g., Y, Hf), residual microstructural inhomogeneities, or extended exposures could alter oxide formation pathways in ways not fully captured by the current design.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare five alloy variants with increasing Al/Cr ratios while holding other principal elements constant. Conduct identical thermal oxidation tests (1000 °C in air, up to 100 h, with repeated cycles), measuring weight changes and characterizing oxide layers via SEM/EDS and XRD.
measurements: Mass gain and oxidation kinetics via thermogravimetric analysis
Morphological and compositional analyses of oxide scales by SEM/EDS
Scale adhesion or spallation upon cooling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any Al- and Cr-enriched alloy does not exhibit a more protective oxide (i.e., it forms transient or poorly adherent oxides) and fails to outperform the low-Al/Cr baseline in oxidation kinetics or scale durability, this would contradict the proposed synergy-driven mechanistic hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: AlCoCrFeNi alloy is a typical type of HEA, and its oxidation resistance has been attracting much attention. It has been found that Al2O3 and Cr2O3 scales are formed on AlxCoCrFeNi alloys due to the selective oxidation of Al and Cr at high temperatures [,,,,]. Alloys can have greater oxidation resistance if the continuity and internal position of the Al2O3 scales are improved by enhancing the content of Al []. Lu concluded that the oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi alloys would be slower if small amounts of Y and Hf were added []. Their oxidation behavior was studied by Butler and Weaver in dry air at 1050 °C []. It has been suggested that they are the perfect material for high-temperature constructional praxis as they have strong oxidation resistance and structural stability. Therefore, AlCoCrFeNi alloys have been proposed as high performance antioxidant coating materials for protecting the high temperature components of aero-engines or as bonded coating materials in TBCs. Cheng prepared AlCoCrFeNi coatings using plasma spraying, and their phase composition could be changed with different spraying power and plasma gas []. Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. The so-called high-entropy alloys based on the refractory elements (refractory high-entropy alloys, RHEAs) are considered as candidates for high-temperature applications [,,,,]. Some of them have high strength at T ≥ 1000 °C and thus can potentially operate at higher temperatures than commercial nickel-based superalloys [,,,,,,,,,]. Some RHEAs are sufficiently ductile at room temperature even in tension [,,,,] and can be cold rolled [,,,]. However, refractory elements and their alloys are generally vulnerable to oxidation. A number of studies focused on oxidation behavior of different RHEAs [,,,,,,,,,,] have demonstrated that some of them possess much better oxidation resistance than conventional refractory alloys; however, the oxidation behavior strongly depended on the alloy composition and testing conditions. Note that the vast majority of the performed research was conducted at temperatures of T ≥ 1000 °C [,,,,,,].

occupying_moves.lever: systematic variation of key oxide-forming elements (e.g., Al, Cr) in the HEA composition
occupying_moves.technique: high-temperature oxidation tests with thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), XRD, SEM/EDS characterization
occupying_moves.conditions: air or controlled oxygen partial pressure, 800–1200 °C, isothermal and cyclic exposure

chosen.lever: content of Al and Cr (and other reactive elements) in the alloy
chosen.technique: systematic TGA and structural/chemical characterization (XRD, SEM/EDS) after high-temperature exposures
chosen.conditions: variable Al/Cr contents in a model HEA, with repeated oxidation cycles at 1000 °C in controlled atmosphere
chosen.why: Varying the fraction of key oxide-forming elements and characterizing the resulting oxide scales directly tests whether multi-component synergy governs protective oxide stability in high-entropy alloys—this is a well-established approach to pinpoint the compositional drivers of oxidation resistance.
